subject: Partial Differential Equations

projects.title: Weak Maximum Principle and Dirichlet Uniqueness
projects.idea: A non-strict differential inequality does not directly rule out an interior maximum. Add a small strictly subharmonic quadratic, then remove the perturbation.
projects.target: Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d be a nonempty bounded open set and u∈C2(Ω)∩C(Ω¯)u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega). If Δu≥0\Delta u\ge0 in Ω\Omega, prove max⁡Ω¯u=max⁡∂Ωu\max_{\overline\Omega}u=\max_{\partial\Omega}u. Deduce uniqueness in this class for a prescribed Laplacian and prescribed continuous boundary values. No boundary smoothness or connectedness is needed for this weak principle.
imports: Use compact attainment of extrema on closed bounded subsets of Euclidean space. At an interior local maximum of a C2C^2 function, each pure second derivative is nonpositive, hence so is the Laplacian. The bounded open set has compact nonempty boundary. This is a maximum-location result, not the strong maximum principle about interior constancy.

nodes.title: Force strict subharmonicity
nodes.role: Use the positive Laplacian of the quadratic to contradict the second-derivative test at an interior maximum. Local obligation: max⁡Ω¯uε=max⁡∂Ωuε\max_{\overline\Omega}u_\varepsilon=\max_{\partial\Omega}u_\varepsilon.
nodes.inputs: uε(x)=u(x)+ε∥x∥2u_\varepsilon(x)=u(x)+\varepsilon\|x\|^2 with ε>0\varepsilon>0.
nodes.gate: The maximum exists on the compact closure; Δuε≥2dε>0\Delta u_\varepsilon\ge2d\varepsilon>0 rules out every interior maximizing point.
nodes.repair: If Δu≥0\Delta u\ge0 alone is claimed to contradict an interior maximum, restore the strictly positive perturbation first. Withhold this export and recheck its descendants after a versioned correction.
activities: The perturbed function is continuous on the compact closure, so it attains a maximum. At an interior maximum its Hessian has nonpositive diagonal entries, giving Δuε≤0\Delta u_\varepsilon\le0.
But Δuε=Δu+2dε>0\Delta u_\varepsilon=\Delta u+2d\varepsilon>0 everywhere inside. Hence no maximizing point is interior; a maximizing point lies on the boundary, proving the export.

projects.proof:
N1 — Force strict subharmonicity

  1. N1.1. The perturbed function is continuous on the compact closure, so it attains a maximum. At an interior maximum its Hessian has nonpositive diagonal entries, giving Δuε≤0\Delta u_\varepsilon\le0.

  2. N1.2. But Δuε=Δu+2dε>0\Delta u_\varepsilon=\Delta u+2d\varepsilon>0 everywhere inside. Hence no maximizing point is interior; a maximizing point lies on the boundary, proving the export.

N2 — Remove the perturbation

  1. N2.1. For every x∈Ω¯x\in\overline\Omega, E1 gives u(x)≤uε(x)≤max⁡∂Ωu+εR2u(x)\le u_\varepsilon(x)\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u+\varepsilon R^2. Let ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow0 to obtain u(x)≤max⁡∂Ωuu(x)\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u.

  2. N2.2. Taking the maximum over the closure gives one inequality, and inclusion of the boundary in the closure gives the reverse. This proves the maximum principle.

N3 — Compare two solutions

  1. N3.1. The difference w=u−vw=u-v has Δw=0\Delta w=0 and zero boundary values. Apply E2 to ww to get w≤0w\le0.

  2. N3.2. Apply it to −w-w, whose Laplacian also vanishes, to get −w≤0-w\le0. Thus w=0w=0. This proves uniqueness without asserting existence for arbitrary data.
projects.example: On the unit disk in ℝ2\mathbb R^2, u(x,y)=x2+y2u(x,y)=x^2+y^2 has Δu=4\Delta u=4 and maximum one on the boundary. For harmonic boundary data given by the restriction of xx, the function u(x,y)=xu(x,y)=x is a solution, and the comparison argument proves it is the only one in the stated class.
boundary: Boundedness cannot simply be dropped. On the upper half-plane, u(x,y)=yu(x,y)=y is harmonic and continuous up to the boundary, where it is zero, but it is positive and unbounded inside. Compact maximum attainment and the uniform perturbation bound both fail.

projects.title: Existence and Uniqueness for the Weak Poisson Problem
projects.idea: The gradient form becomes an inner product once a Poincaré estimate controls the missing L2L^2 part. Riesz representation then constructs the weak solution directly.
projects.target: Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d be nonempty, bounded, and open, and let real f∈L2(Ω)f\in L^2(\Omega). Prove there is a unique u∈H01(Ω)u\in H_0^1(\Omega) such that ∫Ω∇u⋅∇v=∫Ωfv\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\int_\Omega fv for every v∈H01(Ω)v\in H_0^1(\Omega). If Ω\Omega lies inside a cube of side LL, prove ∥∇u∥2≤L∥f∥2\|\nabla u\|_2\le L\|f\|_2. This is a weak solution of −Δu=f-\Delta u=f with zero boundary condition encoded by H01H_0^1.
imports: Define H1(Ω)H^1(\Omega) as the L2L^2 functions whose distributional first derivatives lie in L2L^2, with norm squared ∥u∥22+∥∇u∥22\|u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2. Import completeness of this Sobolev space; H01H_0^1 is the closure of Cc∞(Ω)C_c^\infty(\Omega) in that norm. Import the real Hilbert-space Riesz theorem FA-03: a bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space is inner product with a unique vector, of equal norm. Use Cauchy–Schwarz, Fubini on smooth functions, and the one-dimensional fundamental theorem. The needed Poincaré bound is proved here.

nodes.title: Establish the energy space
nodes.role: Integrate along one coordinate to prove Poincaré, then use density and equivalent norms. Local obligation: ∥v∥2≤L∥∇v∥2\|v\|_2\le L\|\nabla v\|_2 on H01H_0^1, and a(u,v)=∫∇u⋅∇va(u,v)=\int\nabla u\cdot\nabla v is a complete inner product there.
nodes.inputs: A cube QQ of side LL containing Ω\Omega and smooth compactly supported test functions extended by zero to QQ.
nodes.export: ∥v∥2≤L∥∇v∥2\|v\|_2\le L\|\nabla v\|_2 on H01H_0^1, and a(u,v)=∫∇u⋅∇va(u,v)=\int\nabla u\cdot\nabla v is a complete inner product there.
nodes.gate: Zero extension is used first only for compactly supported smooth functions; the general inequality follows by the defining closure.
nodes.repair: If the gradient seminorm is called a norm without justification, prove Poincaré first; constants are not automatically excluded in other Sobolev spaces. Withhold this export and recheck its descendants after a versioned correction.
activities: After translating the cube, take Q=(0,L)dQ=(0,L)^d. For v∈Cc∞(Ω)v\in C_c^\infty(\Omega) extended by zero, v(x1,x′)=∫0x1∂1v(s,x′)dsv(x_1,x')=\int_0^{x_1}\partial_1v(s,x')\,ds. Cauchy–Schwarz gives |v(x1,x′)|2≤L∫0L|∂1v(s,x′)|2ds|v(x_1,x')|^2\le L\int_0^L|\partial_1v(s,x')|^2ds. Integrate over x1x_1 and x′x' to obtain ∥v∥22≤L2∥∂1v∥22≤L2∥∇v∥22\|v\|_2^2\le L^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2\le L^2\|\nabla v\|_2^2.

Approximate any v∈H01v\in H_0^1 by such smooth functions in the H1H^1 norm. Passing to the norm limit preserves the inequality. Therefore ∥∇v∥2=0\|\nabla v\|_2=0 forces v=0v=0, and the gradient norm is equivalent to the complete H1H^1 norm on its closed subspace H01H_0^1. A gradient-Cauchy sequence is H1H^1-Cauchy by the inequality and converges in both norms. Thus aa is a Hilbert inner product.

projects.example: On Ω=(0,1)\Omega=(0,1) with f=1f=1, let u(x)=x(1−x)/2u(x)=x(1-x)/2. It belongs to H01H_0^1: smooth cutoffs near the endpoints converge in H1H^1, since uu vanishes linearly there and the cutoff-derivative errors are supported on intervals of vanishing length. It satisfies −u″=1-u''=1. Integration by parts against smooth compactly supported vv gives ∫u′v′=∫v\int u'v'=\int v, and density extends this to all H01H_0^1. Its energy norm is ∥u′∥2=1/12≤1=L∥f∥2\|u'\|_2=1/\sqrt{12}\le1=L\|f\|_2.

Testing the same proposed equation with v=1v=1 would require ∫f=0\int f=0, a compatibility condition absent from the Dirichlet theorem. Changing the space changes the problem.

projects.title: Energy Decay and Uniqueness for the Heat Equation
projects.idea: The squared L2L^2 difference is an energy. Its derivative is the negative of a nonnegative gradient integral, so identical initial states cannot separate.
projects.target: Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d be bounded with C1C^1 boundary, T>0T>0, and κ>0\kappa>0. Suppose real u,vu,v have continuous spatial derivatives through order two and time derivative through order one on Ω¯×[0,T]\overline\Omega\times[0,T], solve ut−κΔu=vt−κΔvu_t-\kappa\Delta u=v_t-\kappa\Delta v, and agree on the lateral boundary. Prove ∥u(⋅,t)−v(⋅,t)∥22+2κ∫0t∥∇(u−v)(⋅,s)∥22ds=∥u(⋅,0)−v(⋅,0)∥22\|u(\cdot,t)-v(\cdot,t)\|_2^2+2\kappa\int_0^t\|\nabla(u-v)(\cdot,s)\|_2^2ds=\|u(\cdot,0)-v(\cdot,0)\|_2^2. In particular equal initial data imply u=vu=v.
imports: Use differentiation under an integral for continuous derivatives on the compact cylinder, Green’s integration-by-parts identity on the C1C^1 domain for the stated regularity, and the fundamental theorem of calculus. The difference w=u−vw=u-v solves a homogeneous heat equation with zero boundary values. No existence result or unbounded-domain uniqueness is asserted here.

N1 — Differentiate and dissipate

  1. N1.1. The regularity and compactness allow E′(t)=2∫Ωwwt=2κ∫ΩwΔwE'(t)=2\int_\Omega w w_t=2\kappa\int_\Omega w\Delta w.

projects.proof:
N1 — Integrate along characteristics

  1. N1.1. The chain rule gives utt−c2uxx=−4c2Uξηu_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=-4c^2U_{\xi\eta}, so the mixed derivative vanishes on η>ξ\eta>\xi. For fixed ξ\xi, Uξ(ξ,η)U_\xi(\xi,\eta) is constant on the connected interval η>ξ\eta>\xi. Denote it by a(ξ)a(\xi); locally one can evaluate at a fixed admissible η\eta, so aa is C1C^1.

  2. N1.2. Choose an antiderivative AA of aa. Then U−AU-A has zero ξ\xi derivative. For each fixed η\eta, the interval ξ<η\xi<\eta is connected, so U(ξ,η)−A(ξ)U(\xi,\eta)-A(\xi) depends only on η\eta; call it B(η)B(\eta). Local evaluation shows BB is C2C^2. Thus U=A+BU=A+B on the half-plane. Continuity extends the corresponding identities to t=0t=0.

N2 — Match and verify both initial conditions

  1. N2.1. At t=0t=0, A(x)+B(x)=f(x)A(x)+B(x)=f(x) and −cA′(x)+cB′(x)=g(x)-cA'(x)+cB'(x)=g(x). Differentiating the first identity and solving gives A′=(f′−g/c)/2A'=(f'-g/c)/2, B′=(f′+g/c)/2B'=(f'+g/c)/2. If G(x)=∫0xg(s)dsG(x)=\int_0^x g(s)ds, integration gives A=f/2−G/(2c)+CA=f/2-G/(2c)+C and B=f/2+G/(2c)−CB=f/2+G/(2c)-C.

  2. N2.2. Substitution at x−ctx-ct and x+ctx+ct cancels CC and gives d’Alembert’s formula. Conversely these A,BA,B are C2C^2 because f∈C2f\in C^2 and G∈C2G\in C^2. Each traveling wave satisfies utt=c2uxxu_{tt}=c^2u_{xx} by direct differentiation, and the two initial identities hold. Thus a solution exists and every candidate equals it, proving uniqueness.

N3 — Read the domain of dependence

  1. N3.1. The formula uses ff only at the two endpoints and gg only inside the closed interval. Therefore two admissible initial data sets agreeing on that interval produce the same value at (x,t)(x,t).

  2. N3.2. If f,gf,g vanish outside [−R,R][-R,R] and x>R+ctx>R+ct, then the entire integration interval and both endpoints lie to the right of RR, so every term is zero. The same holds for x<−R−ctx<-R-ct. Hence the support at time tt is contained in the enlarged interval, proving finite propagation.
